A claw is a hard, sharp, curved nail found at the tip of an animal's toe or finger. Think of it like a human fingernail — but much tougher, much sharper, and curved like a hook. Claws are made of keratin, the same material your own nails are made of.

The key features that define a claw:

  • It is hard (not soft like skin)
  • It is pointed at the tip
  • It is curved, like a small hook or a crescent
  • It sits at the very end of a toe or finger (digit)

The word "claw" applies across a wide range of animals, but it looks and works differently depending on the animal.

Cats and other predatory mammals

Cats have some of the most iconic claws. A cat's claw is slender, sharply curved, and blade-like. What makes cats special is that their claws are retractable — the cat can pull them back inside the paw so they stay sharp and don't wear down when walking. When a cat hunts, plays, or defends itself, it extends the claws outward. Big cats like lions, tigers, and leopards have the same kind of claws, just much larger and more powerful.

Dogs, bears, and other mammals

Dogs and bears also have claws, but unlike cats, theirs are non-retractable — they always stay out. Dog claws tend to be blunter and less hooked than cat claws because they constantly touch the ground while walking and gradually wear down. Bear claws, on the other hand, can be very long and strong — a grizzly bear's claws can be several inches long, used for digging, tearing into logs to find insects, and catching fish.

Birds

Birds have claws too, though on birds they are often called talons — especially on birds of prey like eagles, hawks, and owls. A bird's talons are thick, strongly curved, and extremely powerful. An eagle uses its talons to snatch fish out of water or grip prey tightly mid-flight. Even ordinary birds like sparrows and pigeons have claws — smaller and less dramatic, but still sharply curved, helping them perch and grip branches without slipping.

Crabs and lobsters

Here the word "claw" takes on a slightly different form. A crab or lobster has what are called pincers — two-part gripping appendages at the front of their body. Each pincer has two parts that close against each other like a pair of tongs or scissors. This gripping structure is also called a claw. A lobster, for instance, has two such claws — one broader and flatter (used for crushing) and one thinner and sharper (used for cutting and grabbing). These claws are used for defense, catching food, and sometimes fighting other lobsters.

Insects and spiders

Many insects and spiders have tiny claws at the tips of their legs. These are very small and often hook-like, helping them grip surfaces — which is why a fly can walk upside down on a ceiling. These are still called claws, though the word is less commonly used in everyday conversation for these tiny creatures.

Sometimes, especially when describing birds or reptiles, the entire foot — including the toes and nails together — is referred to as a claw. So when someone says "the eagle's claw gripped the branch," they may mean the whole foot, not just one nail. This is a natural extension of the word when the foot itself looks hook-like or grasping.

Because of its distinctive hooked, gripping shape, the word "claw" is also used for tools and machines that look or function like an animal's claw.

  • A claw hammer has a forked, curved end (opposite the striking face) that is used to grip nailheads and pull nails out of wood. That curved, two-pronged end is literally called "the claw."
  • Heavy machinery used in construction or demolition sometimes uses a claw — a large, hinged gripping device at the end of a crane arm that can grab, crush, or lift heavy objects like cars or debris.
  • In arcade machines, there is often a claw — a mechanical three-pronged grip that descends to try to pick up a toy. It is called a claw because it looks and moves just like an animal's gripping appendage.

"Claw" is also used in a figurative sense to describe something gripping, trapping, or controlling in a threatening way — just as an animal's claw grips and holds prey.

  • "She felt the claws of anxiety tighten around her." — Here, anxiety is described as a predator gripping the person.
  • "He finally escaped the claws of his controlling boss." — The boss's control is compared to claws that trap and hold.
  • "The city had sunk into the claws of corruption." — Corruption is imagined as a beast gripping the city.

In these uses, the claw represents power over someone, entrapment, or a grip that is difficult to escape.

There is also the common phrase "get your claws into someone", which means to gain strong influence or control over a person — often with a slightly negative or manipulative implication.

To put it all together, when you see the word claw used as a noun, it can refer to:

  1. The sharp, hard, curved nail at the tip of an animal's toe — the most common meaning.
  2. The entire grasping foot of a bird or reptile.
  3. The pincer of a crab, lobster, or similar creature.
  4. A tool or machine shaped and used like an animal's claw (e.g., the back of a claw hammer).
  5. Figuratively, something that grips, traps, or controls — usually in a threatening or suffocating way.

In all of these uses, the word carries the same underlying idea: something hard, curved, and gripping — something built to hold on.
